entries.clinicalQuestion_ko: 급성 저산소성 호흡부전 성인 환자에서 high-flow nasal cannula를 통한 산소 공급이 표준 산소요법에 비해 삽관(intubation)과 28일 사망률을 감소시키는가?

pico.population: [France] Patients who had acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, with a ratio of the partial pressure of arterial oxygen to the fraction of inspired oxygen (PaO2/FiO2) of 200 or less, a respiratory rate of more than 25 breaths per minute, and pulmonary infiltrate on chest imaging; 1116 patients underwent randomization and 1110 (556 high-flow-oxygen, 554 standard-oxygen) were analyzed. Registry inclusion: patients older than 18 years; exclusions included PaCO2 >45 mmHg, need for emergent intubation, hemodynamic instability (vasopressors >0.3 µg/kg/min), and Glasgow Coma Scale ≤12.
pico.intervention: Oxygen delivered through a high-flow nasal cannula (high-flow-oxygen therapy); n=556 analyzed.
pico.comparison: Standard-oxygen therapy; n=554 analyzed.
pico.outcome: Primary outcome was death by day 28: 14.6% (81 of 556) in the high-flow-oxygen group vs 14.6% (81 of 554) in the standard-oxygen group (difference, -0.05 percentage points; 95% CI, -4.21 to 4.10; P = 0.98).

pico_ko.population: [프랑스] 급성 저산소성 호흡부전 환자로, PaO2/FiO2 비 200 이하, 호흡수 분당 25회 초과, 흉부 영상에서 폐 침윤(pulmonary infiltrate)을 동반한 환자; 1116명이 무작위배정되었고 1110명(high-flow-oxygen 556명, standard-oxygen 554명)이 분석됨. 등록부 기준: 18세 초과 환자; 제외 기준으로 PaCO2 >45 mmHg, 응급 삽관 필요, 혈역학적 불안정(vasopressor >0.3 µg/kg/min), Glasgow Coma Scale ≤12 등이 포함됨.
pico_ko.intervention: High-flow nasal cannula를 통한 산소 공급(high-flow-oxygen 요법); 분석 대상 556명.
pico_ko.comparison: 표준 산소요법(standard-oxygen therapy); 분석 대상 554명.
pico_ko.outcome: 일차 결과는 28일째 사망: high-flow-oxygen군 14.6%(556명 중 81명) vs standard-oxygen군 14.6%(554명 중 81명) (차이 -0.05 percentage points; 95% CI, -4.21 ~ 4.10; P = 0.98).

keyFindings: 28-day mortality was identical between groups: 14.6% (81/556) with high-flow oxygen vs 14.6% (81/554) with standard oxygen (difference -0.05 percentage points; 95% CI -4.21 to 4.10; P=0.98).
Intubation by day 28 was lower with high-flow oxygen: 42.4% (236/556) vs 48.4% (268/554) (difference -5.93 percentage points; 95% CI -11.78 to -0.08).
Serious adverse events (cardiac arrest or pneumothorax) during spontaneous breathing were numerically more frequent with high-flow oxygen: 13 (2.3%) vs 6 (1.1%).
keyFindings_ko: 28일 사망률은 두 군에서 동일했음: high-flow oxygen 14.6%(81/556) vs standard oxygen 14.6%(81/554) (차이 -0.05 percentage points; 95% CI -4.21 ~ 4.10; P=0.98).
28일째 삽관은 high-flow oxygen군에서 더 낮았음: 42.4%(236/556) vs 48.4%(268/554) (차이 -5.93 percentage points; 95% CI -11.78 ~ -0.08).
자발호흡 중 중대한 이상반응(cardiac arrest 또는 pneumothorax)은 high-flow oxygen군에서 수치상 더 많았음: 13명(2.3%) vs 6명(1.1%).

entries.clinicalQuestion_ko: 패혈성 쇼크 환자에서 적혈구(RBC) 수혈(특히 제한적 Hb 역치를 넘어선 수혈)이 원내 사망률을 개선하는가, 그리고 상승된 lactate 수치가 수혈 결정을 안내하는 생리학적 트리거로 쓰일 수 있는가?

pico.population: [South Korea] Adults (age ≥ 19 years) with septic shock presenting to the emergency departments of 16 teaching hospitals, from a prospective multicenter Korean Shock Society (KoSS) registry collected October 2015–December 2022; 8,711 patients included (4 excluded for missing initial Hb), stratified into Hb < 7.0 g/dL (n=535), Hb 7.0–8.9 g/dL (n=1,599), and Hb ≥ 9.0 g/dL (n=6,577).
pico.intervention: RBC transfusion administered within the first six hours of the ED visit (received by 884/8,711, 10.1%; 510/884 [57.7%] transfused at Hb ≥ 7 g/dL and 140/884 [15.8%] at Hb ≥ 9.0 g/dL).
pico.comparison: No RBC transfusion within six hours of the ED visit, within the same Hb stratum.
pico.outcome: In-hospital mortality (multivariable logistic regression, adjusted): no significant association in the Hb < 7.0 g/dL group (aOR 0.86; 95% CI 0.54–1.37) or Hb 7.0–8.9 g/dL group (aOR 0.79; 95% CI 0.59–1.06); in the Hb ≥ 9.0 g/dL group RBC transfusion was associated with increased in-hospital mortality (aOR 1.99; 95% CI 1.34–2.93). Benefits of transfusion were not confirmed on analysis based on lactate level.

pico_ko.population: [대한민국] 응급실에 내원한 성인(만 19세 이상) 패혈성 쇼크 환자로, 16개 수련병원에서 전향적으로 수집된 다기관 Korean Shock Society(KoSS) 레지스트리(2015년 10월~2022년 12월) 대상; 총 8,711명 포함(초기 Hb 결측 4명 제외), Hb < 7.0 g/dL(n=535), Hb 7.0–8.9 g/dL(n=1,599), Hb ≥ 9.0 g/dL(n=6,577)로 층화.
pico_ko.intervention: 응급실 내원 후 첫 6시간 이내에 시행한 RBC 수혈(884/8,711명, 10.1%가 시행; 이 중 510명[57.7%]은 Hb ≥ 7 g/dL에서, 140명[15.8%]은 Hb ≥ 9.0 g/dL에서 수혈).
pico_ko.comparison: 같은 Hb 층 내에서 응급실 내원 후 6시간 이내 RBC 수혈을 받지 않은 군.
pico_ko.outcome: 원내 사망률(다변량 logistic regression, 보정): Hb < 7.0 g/dL 군(aOR 0.86; 95% CI 0.54–1.37)과 Hb 7.0–8.9 g/dL 군(aOR 0.79; 95% CI 0.59–1.06)에서는 유의한 연관 없음; Hb ≥ 9.0 g/dL 군에서는 RBC 수혈이 원내 사망률 증가와 연관(aOR 1.99; 95% CI 1.34–2.93). Lactate 수치 기반 분석에서도 수혈의 이득은 확인되지 않음.

keyFindings: Among 8,711 septic shock patients, 10.1% (884) received RBC transfusion within 6 hours, and 57.7% (510/884) of these were transfused at Hb ≥ 7 g/dL — above the restrictive threshold.

RBC transfusion showed no mortality association in the Hb < 7.0 g/dL (aOR 0.86, 95% CI 0.54–1.37) or Hb 7.0–8.9 g/dL groups (aOR 0.79, 95% CI 0.59–1.06), but was associated with increased in-hospital mortality in the Hb ≥ 9.0 g/dL group (aOR 1.99, 95% CI 1.34–2.93).
Transfused patients in the Hb ≥ 9.0 g/dL group had higher initial lactate (median 5.3 vs. 3.5 mmol/L), yet transfusion benefit was not confirmed in lactate-based analysis.
keyFindings_ko: 패혈성 쇼크 환자 8,711명 중 10.1%(884명)가 6시간 이내 RBC 수혈을 받았고, 이 중 57.7%(510/884)는 제한적 역치를 초과한 Hb ≥ 7 g/dL에서 수혈받았다.
RBC 수혈은 Hb < 7.0 g/dL 군(aOR 0.86, 95% CI 0.54–1.37) 및 Hb 7.0–8.9 g/dL 군(aOR 0.79, 95% CI 0.59–1.06)에서는 사망률과 연관이 없었으나, Hb ≥ 9.0 g/dL 군에서는 원내 사망률 증가와 연관되었다(aOR 1.99, 95% CI 1.34–2.93).
Hb ≥ 9.0 g/dL 군의 수혈 환자는 초기 lactate가 더 높았지만(중앙값 5.3 vs. 3.5 mmol/L), lactate 기반 분석에서도 수혈의 이득은 확인되지 않았다.
entries.fullText:
### INTRODUCTION
Patients with septic shock often have anemia, which is associated with a poor outcome. Red blood cells (RBCs) play a critical role in oxygen transport, and RBC transfusion has been used in patients with septic shock to improve tissue oxygenation. Transfusions in critically ill patients are also associated with risks, such as circulatory overload, transmission of infectious diseases, and hypersensitivity reactions. Therefore, a careful balance between the benefits and risks is essential for each patient. Current guidelines recommend a restrictive transfusion strategy in patients with sepsis with a hemoglobin (Hb) threshold of 7 g/dL. However, few studies have examined real-world transfusion practices in patients with septic shock, particularly regarding adherence to these guidelines.
The guidelines recommend that decisions regarding RBC transfusion should not solely rely on the Hb level, but should also consider individual patient-specific factors and overall clinical condition. However, specific recommendations for alternative physiological transfusion triggers have not been provided. This stems from the limited research into alternative transfusion triggers, compared to the extensive evidence supporting Hb transfusion thresholds. In septic shock, an elevated lactate level indicates inadequate perfusion, and recovery from this condition is critical. However, few studies have reported whether RBC transfusion is beneficial for patients with septic shock and an elevated lactate level.
This study examined RBC transfusion practices in patients with septic shock and investigated the differences in in-hospital mortality rates based on the transfusion status across groups with a different Hb level. Additionally, we explored the relationship between transfusion and mortality based on the lactate level in patients with septic shock. We aimed to investigate transfusion practices in patients with septic shock and to examine whether lactate can be used as a physiological marker to trigger transfusion.

### METHODS

### Data source and study cohort
An observational study was conducted using data from a multicenter registry of the Korean Shock Society (KoSS), prospectively collected between October 2015 and December 2022. The KoSS is a collaborative research network dedicated to improving the diagnosis and management of septic shock. The registry includes data collected from patients with septic shock who presented to the emergency departments (EDs) of 16 teaching hospitals in South Korea.
The inclusion criteria for patients in the KoSS registry were: age ≥ 19 years, visit to participating ED with suspected or confirmed infection, and evidence of refractory hypotension or hypoperfusion. Hypotension was defined as systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg, mean arterial pressure (MAP) < 70 mmHg, or a reduction of > 40 mmHg in systolic blood pressure. Refractory hypotension was defined as persistent hypotension following administration of intravenous fluid (≥ 1L over 30 minutes or 20–30 mL/kg) or the requirement for vasopressors after fluid resuscitation. Hypoperfusion was defined as a serum lactate level ≥ 4 mmol/L. This differs from the Sepsis-3 definition of septic shock, as the KoSS registry began prior to the implementation of the Sepsis-3 definition. Patients who were classified as “Do Not Attempt Resuscitation” at the time of the ED visit, diagnosed more than six hours after the ED visit, or transferred to another hospital during ED treatment were excluded.
Patients with a missing initial Hb value in the registry were excluded. Patients with septic shock were divided into three groups based on their initial Hb level: Hb < 7.0 g/dL, Hb 7.0–8.9 g/dL, and Hb ≥ 9.0 g/dL. Group classification was based on an Hb level of 7 g/dL for the restrictive transfusion threshold and 9 g/dL for the liberal transfusion threshold.

### Data collection
Demographic and clinical data including age, sex, initial Hb and lactate levels, initial vital signs, medical history, and infection focus were extracted from the KoSS registry. The severity of illness was assessed using the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score and the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II) score at the time of patient enrollment. The presence of septic shock, as defined by the Sepsis-3 criteria, was also determined. Sepsis-3 shock refers to sepsis with persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain a MAP ≥ 65 mmHg and a serum lactate level > 2 mmol/L, despite adequate fluid resuscitation.
During the initial period following an ED visit, patients with septic shock often present with unstable vital signs, reflecting the acute phase. During this critical period, fluid resuscitation, administration of antibiotics, and vasopressor therapy are essential interventions that can significantly reduce mortality. The KoSS registry includes variables regarding whether RBC transfusions were administered within six hours and 24 hours of the ED visit. To assess whether RBC transfusion during the acute resuscitation phase was associated with patient outcomes, the independent variable in this study was defined as the administration of RBC transfusion within the first six hours of the ED visit.
To account for the overall quality of septic shock management, we also collected data on adherence to the sepsis resuscitation bundle. These data included the time to antibiotic administration (categorized as < 1 hour, 1–3 hours, or ≥ 3 hours from the ED visit), whether at least 30 mL/kg of crystalloid fluid was administered within 3 hours, the achievement of a MAP > 65 mmHg (typically with vasopressors within 6 hours), and whether source control interventions, such as emergency surgery or percutaneous drainage, were performed.
The primary outcome of this study was in-hospital mortality. First, whether in-hospital mortality differed between the transfusion and non-transfusion groups based on the Hb level was assessed. Subsequently, this outcome was examined within subgroups categorized by the lactate level.

### Statistical analysis
Categorical variables are presented as counts and percentages. Fisher’s exact test was used to compare categorical variables between two groups. The normality of continuous variables was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Continuous variables with a normal distribution are presented as means and standard deviations, whereas those with a non-normal distribution are presented as medians and interquartile ranges (25th to 75th percentiles). The Student’s -test or the Wilcoxon rank-sum test was applied based on the results of the test for normality.
To evaluate the association between RBC transfusion within six hours and in-hospital mortality, multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed. The model was adjusted for potential confounding factors that might influence in-hospital mortality. These covariates included age, sex, SOFA score, APACHE II score, initial lactate level, and compliance with the sepsis bundle, specifically: timing of antibiotics, adequate fluid administration, use of vasopressors to maintain MAP > 65 mmHg, and source control. The results are presented as adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). All statistical analyses were conducted using R software (version 4.4.1; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) with the R Studio interface. Statistical significance was determined using two-sided, unpaired tests with a  value < 0.05.

### Ethics statement
This study was approved by the Institutional Review Boards of Hanyang University Hospital (HYUH 2015-11-013-022), and informed consent was obtained before data collection. The study has therefore been performed in accordance with the ethical standards laid down in the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its later amendments.

### RESULTS

### Basic characteristics of transfused patients
Of the 8,715 patients registered in the KoSS registry, four with missing Hb data were excluded, resulting in 8,711 being included in the analysis (). Among these, 535 patients had Hb < 7.0 g/dL, 1,599 had Hb 7.0–8.9 g/dL, and 6,577 had Hb ≥ 9.0 g/dL. The percentage of patients who received an RBC transfusion was 10.1% (884/8,711). For patients with Hb < 7.0 g/dL, Hb 7.0–8.9 g/dL, and Hb ≥ 9.0 g/dL, 69.9% (374/535), 23.1% (370/1,599), and 2.1% (140/6,577), respectively, received an RBC transfusion. Among the 884 patients who received an RBC transfusion, 510 (57.7%) were transfused at an Hb level ≥ 7 g/dL, exceeding the restrictive threshold (). Furthermore, 15.8% (140/884) of the patients who received an RBC transfusion were transfused at an Hb level ≥ 9.0 g/dL, which exceeds the liberal transfusion threshold.
To identify the factors associated with RBC transfusion, the baseline characteristics were compared between the transfusion and non-transfusion groups (). For the patients in the Hb 7.0–8.9 g/dL and Hb ≥ 9.0 g/dL groups, the transfusion group was younger than the non-transfusion group, whereas the Hb < 7.0 g/dL group had a higher percentage of females in the transfusion group. The severity of illness, as indicated by the SOFA score and the APACHE II score, was higher in the transfusion group than in the non-transfusion group across all groups of Hb level. In all groups, the initial Hb level was lower in the transfusion group than in the non-transfusion group. entries.clinicalQuestion_ko: 패혈성 쇼크 및 기타 혈관확장성 상태에서, 대순환의 혈압과 심박출량(cardiac output)이 회복되었음에도 불구하고 왜 이질적인 미세순환 기능장애(haemodynamic incoherence)가 지속되는가, 그리고 이를 혈관확장·유량 제한·shear 조절의 상호작용에서 비롯되는 필연적 결과로 설명하는 기전 모델을 세울 수 있는가?

pico.population: [Country NR] A simulated (in silico) microcirculatory network of one million parallel arterioles in Python (JupyterLab v4.3.4), with vessel radii drawn from a truncated normal distribution (physiological bounds 0–100 microns), mean radius varied 20–30 microns and standard deviation 1.5–3 microns; not human or animal subjects but a computational model of the human microcirculation (true parallel arteriole number probably closer to 100 million, scaled down by a factor of 100 for computation).
pico.intervention: A conceptual and computational model in which each vessel's flow demand (Q) is set by an 'apparent shear target' derived from the laminar shear equation (dynamic viscosity 0.003 Pa·s; apparent shear target 10–20 Pa), with total required cardiac output computed as the sum of individual vessel demands; simulated global vasodilation via rising mean vessel radius (20→30 microns).
pico.comparison: Baseline reference network at a mean vessel radius of 20 microns (no vessel dropout), against which relative network resistance and functional derecruitment at larger mean radii were compared; and comparison of shear targets of 10 vs 20 Pa.
pico.outcome: Minimum cardiac output required to maintain the global shear target rose almost linearly with mean vessel radius (total flow demand proportional to the sum of vessel radii cubed): at shear target 20 Pa and SD 1.5 microns, from ~5 L/min at mean radius 25 microns to ~8.5 L/min at 30 microns. No comparative statistics (no OR/HR/CI/p-values) were reported — this is a deterministic simulation.

pico_ko.population: [국가 미기재] Python(JupyterLab v4.3.4)으로 시뮬레이션한 100만 개 평행 세동맥(arteriole)의 미세순환 네트워크(in silico). 혈관 반지름은 절단 정규분포(생리학적 경계 0–100 microns)에서 추출했고, 평균 반지름 20–30 microns, 표준편차 1.5–3 microns로 변화시킴. 실제 사람/동물 대상이 아니라 인체 미세순환의 전산 모델이며, 실제 평행 세동맥 수는 약 1억 개에 가깝지만 계산 편의를 위해 100분의 1로 축소함.
pico_ko.intervention: 각 혈관의 유량 요구(Q)를 층류 shear 방정식에서 유도한 'apparent shear target'로 설정한 개념적·전산 모델(dynamic viscosity 0.003 Pa·s, apparent shear target 10–20 Pa). 필요한 총 심박출량은 개별 혈관 요구량의 합으로 계산했고, 평균 혈관 반지름을 20→30 microns로 늘려 전신 혈관확장을 모사함.
pico_ko.comparison: 평균 혈관 반지름 20 microns인 기준 네트워크(혈관 탈락 없음)를 기준으로, 더 큰 평균 반지름에서의 상대적 네트워크 저항 및 기능적 derecruitment를 비교했고, shear target 10 Pa 대 20 Pa도 비교함.
pico_ko.outcome: 전체 shear target을 유지하는 데 필요한 최소 심박출량은 평균 혈관 반지름에 따라 거의 선형으로 증가함(총 유량 요구는 혈관 반지름 세제곱의 합에 비례). shear target 20 Pa, SD 1.5 microns에서 평균 반지름 25 microns일 때 약 5 L/min, 30 microns일 때 약 8.5 L/min. 비교 통계(OR/HR/CI/p-value)는 보고되지 않았으며, 결정론적(deterministic) 시뮬레이션임.

keyFindings: In a one-million-vessel simulation, total cardiac output required to maintain a fixed shear target rises in proportion to the sum of vessel radii cubed, so even modest global vasodilation sharply increases required flow — at shear 20 Pa/SD 1.5 microns, from ~5 L/min (mean radius 25 microns) to ~8.5 L/min (30 microns).

When cardiac output cannot meet demand, low-shear vessels functionally derecruit: increasing mean radius from 25 to 30 microns at a fixed 5000 mL/min caused almost 50% vessel dropout with network resistance falling to 33% of baseline, reproducing the reduced functional capillary density and hyperdynamic, low-resistance circulation of severe sepsis.

Lowering the apparent shear target from 20 to 10 Pa halved the cardiac output requirement, suggesting microvascular coherence could in principle be restored by reducing vasodilation or shear demand rather than by achieving supranormal cardiac output.
keyFindings_ko: 100만 혈관 시뮬레이션에서, 고정된 shear target을 유지하는 데 필요한 총 심박출량은 혈관 반지름 세제곱의 합에 비례해 증가하므로, 경미한 전신 혈관확장만으로도 필요 유량이 급격히 늘어남 — shear 20 Pa/SD 1.5 microns에서 평균 반지름 25 microns일 때 약 5 L/min, 30 microns일 때 약 8.5 L/min.

심박출량이 수요를 못 따라가면 저-shear 혈관이 기능적으로 derecruit됨: 고정 5000 mL/min에서 평균 반지름을 25→30 microns로 늘리자 약 50% 혈관 탈락과 함께 네트워크 저항이 기준의 33%로 떨어졌고, 이는 severe sepsis의 functional capillary density 감소 및 hyperdynamic·저저항 순환을 재현함.
apparent shear target을 20에서 10 Pa로 낮추면 심박출량 요구가 절반으로 감소해, supranormal cardiac output 달성이 아니라 혈관확장이나 shear 수요를 줄임으로써 미세혈관 coherence를 원리적으로 회복할 수 있음을 시사함.

### Background
Sepsis is the most common cause of circulatory failure treated in the intensive care unit. Despite this, a consistent understanding of the pathophysiology has been elusive. At first, it was thought sepsis was a standard low output shock state. Widespread use of the pulmonary artery catheter in the 60s and 70s first revealed the more common hyperdynamic, low resistance situation [, ]. At the same time animal and ex-vivo studies showed widespread arteriolar vasodilation and hypo-responsiveness of micro-vessels to catecholamines and other vasoconstricting agents [, ]. The next several decades of therapeutic theory focussed on enhancing oxygen delivery through targeting ScvO2 and supranormal cardiac index, which ultimately proved fruitless [, ].
Since the turn of the millennium access to new imaging techniques like handheld videomicroscopy has revealed the importance of microcirculatory dysfunction. Capillary perfusion is heterogeneous, with reduced functional capillary density and perfused vessel density, and increased stop flow capillaries [, ]. These changes may persist despite normalisation of macrocirculatory variables such as blood pressure and cardiac output and predict mortality; the so-called haemodynamic incoherence []. A satisfactory explanation for this disconnect has not emerged. Why a global vasodilatory process should lead to such a patchy locally heterogeneous problem is unclear. While it is possible that the two phenomena are completely separate, purely vasodilatory conditions such as calcium channel blocker overdose also result in the same microvascular impairment despite high global flow [].
Shear stress is the force exerted by flowing blood on the endothelium, in the direction parallel to the vessel wall. Shear signalling in normal endothelium involves feedback that maintains shear stress within vessels within a given range. Shear is increased by flow and by a reduction in vessel size. When shear is excessive, the signalling pathway will result in local release of nitric oxide (NO), which dilates the vessel and reduces the shear stress back to an acceptable range. Low shear produces endothelin, which constricts the vessel. Sensing of shear occurs via mechanotransduction proteins in the endothelial glycocalyx and gap junctions. Shear regulation is prominent within the microcirculation [, ].
Shear signalling is known to be abnormal in septic shock. Excessive expression of inducible NO synthase (iNOS) results in elevated levels of NO []. At the same time endothelial damage disrupts mechanotransducers and inflammatory cytokines inhibit signalling pathways, resulting in impairment of shear sensing [, ]. These observations have been linked generally to the development of microvascular dysfunction, but not through a mechanistic hypothesis.
The aim of this paper is to put forward a hypothesis that explains these disparate findings, and model how the microcirculation is constrained by three main factors; total cardiac output, vasomotor state, and shear regulation. Predictable behaviour of the microcirculation naturally emerges from changes in these variables.

### Methods
A microcirculatory network consisting of one million parallel arterioles was simulated in Python using JupyterLab (v 4.3.4). The distribution of vessel radii was simulated with a truncated normal distribution (with lower and upper physiological bounds of 0 and 100 microns). The mean vessel radius was varied between 20 and 30 microns, and the standard deviation between 1.5 and 3 microns, consistent with the typical size of arterioles in the microcirculation []. Typical numbers of parallel arterioles in the human body are unknown exactly, but probably closer to 100 million (based on roughly 10 capillaries and each arteriole feeding a bed of 100 capillaries [, ]), however the simulation was scaled for ease of computation, as explained further below.

The typical value of shear stress in arterioles is unknown, but has been observed to be 1–7 Pa in larger arteries and ten times less in capillaries [, ]. entries.fullText:
### Introduction
Atrial fibrillation (AF), elevated heart rate and elevated plasma cardiac troponin are common manifestations of sepsis-related circulatory stress, yet their clinical significance remains unclear. In practice, troponin elevations during sepsis are often attributed to rate-related demand ischaemia associated with higher heart rates or AF, and structured cardiac follow-up after discharge is not routinely performed. However, no guidelines specifically address management of sepsis-associated myocardial injury, leaving uncertainty for critical care physicians and cardiologists regarding short-term and long-term care.
AF and elevated heart rate are recognised markers of illness severity, but whether they directly contribute to myocardial injury or simply co-occur with troponin elevation remains uncertain. Furthermore, the extent to which plasma high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs-cTnT), AF and heart rate independently or jointly relate to long-term mortality is unknown. To address this gap, we investigated the associations of hs-cTnT, AF and highest recorded heart rate, with 1-year mortality in a cohort of critically ill patients with sepsis.

### Methods

### Study population and trial design
The Sepsis and Elevated Troponin (SET) study was a previously reported single-centre retrospective cohort study evaluating the association between plasma hs-cTnT concentrations and mortality in patients with sepsis or septic shock. Details of patient inclusion are provided in the supplemental material (). The cohort comprised 586 adults with sepsis requiring vasopressor support in the intermediate or intensive care units at Danderyd University Hospital, Stockholm, Sweden, between March 2012 and September 2021. The study was approved by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority.
Patients were identified retrospectively through the electronic health record (EHR). Eligible participants required vasopressor support, fulfilled Sepsis-3 criteria for sepsis or septic shock and had at least one hs-cTnT measurement within 48 hours of sepsis onset. According to Sepsis-3, septic shock was defined as requiring vasopressor therapy to maintain a mean arterial pressure ≥65 mm Hg and serum lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

### Data collection and outcomes
Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics, laboratory and microbiological data, in-hospital treatments and mortality were extracted from the EHR. Frailty was assessed using the Clinical Frailty Scale, comorbidity burden using the Charlson Comorbidity Index and disease severity using the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score. Sepsis onset was defined as the time at which sepsis-related abnormal vital signs were first documented in the EHR.
Electrocardiograms obtained within 8 hours of sepsis onset were classified as normal if sinus rhythm was present with QRS duration ≤0.12 s and no ST-segment or T-wave abnormalities. Patients were classified as having no AF, pre-existing AF (defined by a previously registered International Classification of Diseases [ICD]-10 diagnosis code for AF in the EHR) or new-onset AF (NOAF). AF, whether previously diagnosed or new-onset, was confirmed by ECG or continuous telemetry monitoring within 72 hours of sepsis onset.
Plasma hs-cTnT was analysed at the Karolinska University Laboratory (Stockholm, Sweden) using an electrochemiluminescence assay (Elecsys Assay 2, Roche Diagnostics). Myocardial injury was defined as hs-cTnT above the 99th percentile upper reference limit (≥15 ng/L). Because AF and heart rate evolve dynamically during sepsis, the highest available hs-cTnT value within 48 hours of sepsis onset was used to reflect cumulative myocardial injury. hs-cTnT concentrations were categorised into quartiles: Q1, 15–41 ng/L; Q2, 42–78 ng/L; Q3, 79–184 ng/L; Q4, >184 ng/L.
The highest recorded heart rate within the first 72 hours of sepsis onset was extracted from the EHR using values documented by nursing staff from continuous telemetry monitoring. Heart rate was analysed as a continuous variable in regression models and dichotomised at 120 beats per minute for Kaplan-Meier analyses. This prespecified threshold was based on physiological data demonstrating rising hs-cTnT concentrations above 110–120 beats per minute in patients with AF, aligned with guideline-recommended rate-control targets (<100–110 beats per min), and was consistent with a previous study in septic and cardiogenic shock that used the same cut-off.
The primary analysis examined the association between the highest plasma hs-cTnT and all-cause 1-year mortality in patients with and without AF, adjusting for the highest recorded heart rate. Secondary analyses assessed the contributions of AF and heart rate to variability in hs-cTnT.

### Statistical analysis
Baseline characteristics were summarised according to AF category (no AF, pre-existing AF or NOAF). Continuous variables were reported as mean (SD) for normally distributed data and median (IQR) for non-normally distributed data. Categorical variables were presented as counts and percentages. Between-group comparisons were performed using one-way analysis of variance for normally distributed continuous variables and the Kruskal-Wallis test for non-normally distributed continuous variables. Categorical variables were compared using the χ² test.
Time-to-event for 1-year all-cause mortality was estimated using Kaplan-Meier methods, with group comparisons performed using the log-rank test. For stratified Kaplan-Meier analyses, pre-existing AF and NOAF were combined into a single binary AF variable to facilitate visual presentation.
Univariable and multivariable linear regression analyses were used to assess continuous associations, and natural cubic splines were used to evaluate non-linear relationships. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression evaluated associations with 1-year mortality. A multivariable regression model was constructed to evaluate the associations between AF, heart rate and myocardial injury. Covariates were selected a priori based on clinical relevance and established associations with sepsis mortality. Right-skewed predictors, including hs-cTnT, were natural log-transformed before regression analyses.
Missing data for covariates were negligible. An exception was left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), available in 305 patients (52%) who underwent transthoracic echocardiography during hospitalisation. To retain all patients in multivariable analyses, an ordinal variable was created to capture both echocardiography availability and systolic dysfunction: 0, not performed; 1, preserved LVEF (≥50%); 2, mildly reduced LVEF (40–49%); 3, moderately or severely reduced LVEF (<40%).
All tests were two-sided, with p value <0.05 considered statistically significant. Analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics, V.30.0.0.0 (IBM Corp) and RStudio, V.2024.04.2+764.

### Results

### Baseline characteristics and hospital course
The SET study included 586 patients with sepsis or septic shock requiring vasopressor treatment ().
Patients with AF were older, more frequently male and had greater frailty and cardiovascular comorbidity than those without AF (). Pre-existing AF was associated with a higher burden of chronic cardiovascular disease and lower habitual renal function.
Patients with NOAF demonstrated higher SOFA scores and greater inflammatory burden during sepsis, reflected by higher C reactive protein concentrations. Patients with AF also had higher recorded heart rates, hs-cTnT concentrations and N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide concentrations. Elevated hs-cTnT concentrations were observed in 546 patients (93%), with values ranging from 4 ng/L to 21 900 ng/L. The range of highest recorded heart rates was 60–174 beats per minute in the no AF group, 44–190 beats per minute in the pre-existing AF group and 62–190 beats per minute in the NOAF group.

### Contribution of AF, heart rate and left ventricular function to variation in hs-cTnT levels
AF status was associated with log-transformed hs-cTnT concentrations, but the effect size was small, explaining only 1.2% of the variability in hs-cTnT levels (). Likewise, AF status explained only 2.2% of the variability in highest recorded heart rate (). Heart rate itself was not associated with log-transformed hs-cTnT concentrations and accounted for virtually none of the observed variability (R < 0.001; ). Among patients with echocardiographic data, lower LVEF was associated with higher log-transformed hs-cTnT concentrations and explained 9.4% of the variability in hs-cTnT levels ().

### 1-year mortality by AF, heart rate and troponin
At 1 year, the highest recorded heart rate was not associated with mortality, whether analysed as a continuous variable (HR 1.0; 95% CI 0.99 to 1.004; p=0.580), modelled using natural cubic splines (p=0.303) or dichotomised at 120 beats per minute (). Compared with patients without AF, both pre-existing AF (HR 2.4; 95% CI 1.8 to 3.2; p<0.001) and NOAF (HR 1.8; 95% CI 1.3 to 2.5; p<0.001) were associated with higher 1-year mortality ().
In stratified analyses of AF and heart rate, Kaplan-Meier curves demonstrated marked differences in unadjusted mortality between groups (). Patients with a heart rate ≤120 beats per minute and no AF had the lowest mortality, followed by those with a heart rate >120 beats per minute and no AF. entries.fullText:
### Background
Myocardial injury is common in sepsis and consistently associated with adverse outcomes, yet its underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood [, ]. Coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) has been proposed as a contributing mechanism []. Histopathological studies demonstrate microvascular alterations alongside cardiomyocyte damage, supporting a mechanistic link between coronary microvascular injury and myocardial injury [, ]. However, CMD has not been systematically characterised in vivo in patients with sepsis.
The contribution of obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD) to myocardial injury in sepsis also remains uncertain. Existing angiographic studies have largely been restricted to highly selected patients with suspected acute coronary syndromes, and the frequency of obstructive CAD in patients with sepsis-associated myocardial injury remains poorly defined [–].
Sepsis is fundamentally a disorder of the microcirculation, characterised by widespread endothelial and glycocalyx injury, capillary leak, and impaired microvascular perfusion, leading to multi-organ dysfunction, often with cardiac involvement [, ]. These alterations may manifest within the coronary circulation as acute CMD through impaired vasoreactivity, microvascular obstruction, and interstitial oedema, potentially contributing to myocardial injury [, ].
In this study, we performed invasive coronary angiography and assessment of coronary microvascular function in patients with sepsis and myocardial injury, defined by elevated plasma high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs-cTnT) concentrations. We hypothesised that greater impairment in microvascular function would be associated with higher hs-cTnT concentrations. In addition, we characterised the frequency and physiological phenotypes of CMD in sepsis and evaluated the occurrence of underlying obstructive epicardial CAD. We also explored associations between coronary physiological indices, echocardiographic findings, and cardiac biomarker concentrations.
Coronary microvascular function was quantified using established invasive thermodilution-derived indices, including the index of microcirculatory resistance (IMR) and microvascular resistance reserve (MRR) [, ]. We also compared microvascular findings with those of a matched cohort of patients with chronic coronary syndrome (CCS) to provide physiological context for the magnitude and patterns of CMD observed in sepsis.

### Methods

### Study design and objectives
This prospective observational study aimed to characterise coronary microvascular function in patients with sepsis-associated myocardial injury using invasive thermodilution-based assessment. The primary objective was to examine the association between plasma hs-cTnT concentrations and IMR, an invasive index of hyperaemic coronary microvascular resistance.
Pre-specified secondary objectives were to evaluate the association between plasma hs-cTnT concentrations and obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD), additional thermodilution-derived coronary microvascular indices, and echocardiographic measures of cardiac structure and function. Additional secondary objectives were to characterise the occurrence and physiological phenotypes of CMD.
Exploratory objectives included assessing associations of plasma NT-proBNP concentrations with coronary microvascular indices and echocardiographic measures of cardiac structure and function. Coronary microvascular function in patients with sepsis was also compared with that of a matched control cohort with CCS.

### Patient population
In the  (COMTESS; ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: ; registered March 2, 2024), we prospectively enrolled consecutive adults admitted to the intensive or intermediate care unit at Danderyd University Hospital. All patients with sepsis admitted to these units were prospectively screened for eligibility.
Eligible patients were aged 40–85 years, met the Sepsis-3 diagnostic criteria for sepsis or septic shock, had an expected survival >1 year, and demonstrated myocardial injury, defined as a plasma hs-cTnT concentration ≥ 15 ng/L within 48 h of sepsis onset [, ]. Patients were screened on the basis of hs-cTnT elevation irrespective of symptoms suggestive of acute coronary syndrome or prior suspicion of CAD.
Exclusion criteria included prior coronary artery bypass grafting, pre-admission left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction ≤ 39%, chronic kidney disease with a pre-admission estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) < 30 mL/min/1.73 m², and infective endocarditis. Patients with persistent clinical instability beyond day 8 (ongoing circulatory shock requiring vasopressors or respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support) were excluded. Patients were also excluded when invasive coronary angiography was considered unsafe or unfeasible (full criteria are provided in the Supplementary Methods). Detailed patient screening, enrolment, and reasons for exclusion are shown in Supplementary Figure S1.
Patients underwent coronary angiography with invasive assessment of coronary microvascular function and transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) following clinical stabilisation, between days 2 and 10 after sepsis onset. Invasive assessment was performed after haemodynamic stabilisation to minimise the influence of shock and vasoactive therapy on coronary physiological measurements and to ensure procedural safety.
The study was approved by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority, conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and all participants provided written informed consent.

### Coronary angiography and coronary microvascular assessment
Coronary angiography was performed according to standard clinical protocols. Obstructive CAD was defined as ≥ 50% diameter stenosis or fractional flow reserve (FFR) ≤ 0.80 in an epicardial coronary artery ≥ 2.5 mm in diameter [].
Coronary flow indices were obtained by thermodilution [, , ]. Following administration of ≥ 100 µg intracoronary nitroglycerine, a thermistor-equipped pressure wire (PressureWire™ X, Abbott Vascular Inc., CA, USA) was advanced > 70 mm into the left anterior descending artery (LAD) and connected to dedicated acquisition software (Coroventis Research AB, Uppsala, Sweden).
At rest, three intracoronary bolus injections of saline (3 mL each) were administered to determine mean transit time. Aortic and distal coronary pressures were simultaneously recorded. Maximal hyperaemia was induced using intravenous adenosine (167 µg/kg/min), followed by repeat triplicate saline injections to obtain hyperaemic mean transit time. Hyperaemic aortic and distal coronary pressures were simultaneously recorded [, ].
Resting and hyperaemic coronary blood flow (CBF) were defined as the inverse of mean transit time []. Baseline resistance index (BRI) and index of microcirculatory resistance (IMR) were calculated as measures of resting and hyperaemic microvascular resistance, respectively. Collateral-corrected IMR was used for all analyses to account for flow-limiting CAD [, ]. Microvascular resistance reserve (MRR) was calculated as a pressure-corrected index of coronary microvascular vasodilatory capacity. Unlike coronary flow reserve (CFR), which is influenced by both epicardial and microvascular disease, MRR is a specific index of microvascular vasodilator capacity [, ]. Detailed definitions and calculation formulas are provided in Supplementary Table S1.
CMD was defined as MRR ≤ 3 and/or IMR > 25 according to established invasive coronary physiology thresholds [, ]. Patients were further classified into four physiological phenotypes: no CMD (MRR > 3 and IMR ≤ 25); elevated IMR only (MRR > 3 and IMR > 25); functional CMD (MRR ≤ 3 and IMR ≤ 25); and structural CMD (MRR ≤ 3 and IMR > 25) [, , , ].

### Echocardiography
TTE was performed using Vivid E9 or Vivid E95 ultrasound systems (GE Healthcare) equipped with an M5Sc transducer and analysed according to established guidelines []. Comprehensive echocardiographic assessment of cardiac structure and function was performed by certified sonographers or clinical physiologists and reviewed by a single certified assessor blinded to clinical data.
Detailed echocardiographic acquisition, measurements, thresholds, and classification criteria for diastolic dysfunction are provided in the Supplementary Methods.

### Cardiac biomarkers
Plasma hs-cTnT (Roche Diagnostics, Elecsys Assay 2) and N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP; Roche Diagnostics, Elecsys Assay 3) were measured serially during the first 48 h after sepsis onset. Sampling was intended at approximately 12, 24, and 48 h according to the study protocol. In practice, timing was guided by local routine and clinical indication, and additional samples were often obtained at shorter intervals (1–3 h) to assess dynamic changes. hs-cTnT measurements were repeated until concentrations stabilised or declined, and the highest value recorded during the first 48 h was used to estimate early myocardial injury burden.

### Clinical data collection
Baseline demographics, comorbidities identified from International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) codes recorded prior to admission, in-hospital laboratory results and treatments, primary site of infection, microbiological findings, and vital status were prospectively collected from the electronic health record. Sepsis onset was defined as the earliest documented time at which sepsis-related physiological abnormalities included in the National Early Warning Score 2 were recorded in the electronic health record. A 12-lead electrocardiogram was obtained within four hours of sepsis onset. Atrial fibrillation was confirmed by findings on electrocardiography or continuous telemetry monitoring.

### Control population
Controls matched for age, sex and number of obstructive CAD lesions were selected from a cohort of 506 patients with CCS who underwent clinically indicated elective coronary angiography

### Mechanisms of sepsis-induced immunosuppression

### The functional inhibition of the innate immune system

### Dysfunction of monocytes/macrophages

### Decrease in antigen-presenting ability
During sepsis, the expression of HLA-DR on the surface of monocytes is significantly reduced. HLA-DR belongs to the major histocompatibility complex class II molecules (MHC II), which plays a crucial role in the antigen presentation process. Under normal circumstances, after monocytes uptake antigens such as pathogens, they present the antigen peptide-MHC II complex on the cell surface for T cells to recognize, thereby initiating the adaptive immune response.However, in the state of sepsis, on the one hand, the expression of HLA-DR on the cell surface decreases, reducing the presentation of the antigen peptide-MHC II complex. At the same time, the expression of other costimulatory molecules is abnormal, making it difficult for T cells to normally recognize antigens and be fully activated, which greatly inhibits the adaptive immune response. On the other hand, there is an imbalance in cytokine secretion. The secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF and IL-1β decreases, thus weakening the autoimmune function of monocytes. In contrast, the secretion of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 increases. It inhibits the activation of monocytes and the expression of molecules such as HLA-DR, further suppressing the immune response. Eventually, it leads to a significant decrease in the antigen-presenting ability of monocytes [].
Pediatric considerations: In children with sepsis, monocytes/macrophages exhibit a unique cytokine profile compared to adults. Stimulation of pediatric peritoneal macrophages with LPS results in a 15‑fold higher IL‑10/TNF‑α ratio than that observed in adult macrophages, indicating a stronger anti‑inflammatory feedback propensity. This exaggerated anti‑inflammatory response may predispose children to early immunoparalysis despite a concurrent hyperinflammatory state. Furthermore, HLA‑DR downregulation on monocytes has been documented as early as 72 h after PICU admission in children with severe sepsis, correlating with prolonged organ dysfunction.

### Polarization phenotype transformation
The M2 macrophages are an anti-inflammatory phenotype of macrophages and participate in immunosuppression by secreting interleukin-4 (IL-4) and interleukin-10 (IL-10). IL-4 inhibits the phagocytic and bactericidal functions of macrophages. IL-10 serves as a hub for the interaction among M2 macrophages, regulatory T cells (Tregs), and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) [].M2 macrophage-derived IL-10 drives Treg expansion, while Treg-secreted cytokines reciprocally enhance M2 polarization, establishing a self-amplifying immunosuppressive feedback loop. Moreover, IL-10 also stimulates the expansion of MDSCs by upregulating the expression of programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) and programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) []. MDSCs inhibit the proliferation of T lymphocytes and promote their apoptosis, suppress the maturation of dendritic cells, induce the phenotype of M2 macrophages, and facilitate the expansion of Tregs, collectively exacerbating immunosuppression [].

### Dysfunction of neutrophils

### Decreased chemotaxis
When the body is stimulated by factors such as pathogen invasion or tissue injury, damaged tissue cells and immune cells release inflammatory mediators, such as tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), interleukin-1 (IL-1), etc., which promote the activation of vascular endothelial cells and the expression of adhesion molecules. Neutrophils in the blood circulation adhere tightly to the ligands on the surface of endothelial cells under the action of activation signals such as chemokines. Subsequently, neutrophils migrate through the endothelial cells and penetrate the blood vessel wall, and then chemotactically move along the concentration gradient of chemokines towards the site of inflammation. Once they arrive, they are activated, and they clear pathogens by phagocytosis and releasing bactericidal substances, thus exerting their immune defense function.Numerous studies have shown that although the levels of chemotactic molecules in the infection foci of septic patients and septic mice are relatively high, the number of neutrophils in these areas does not increase significantly, suggesting that there is a dysfunction in the migration of neutrophils during sepsis [, ]. The expression levels of Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), chemokine receptor CXCR2, and other molecules in septic patients who died are often lower than those in septic patients who survived [] (Fig. ).
[object Object]

### Increased release of extracellular traps
Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are composed of DNA, histones, and serine proteases []. The release of NETs by neutrophils enhances vascular inflammation and coagulation, and NET release does not always lead to neutrophil death. NETs can capture pathogens, thus contributing to the elimination of pathogens. However, NETs can also cause collateral tissue damage and thrombosis. Elevated circulating NETs correlate with multi-organ dysfunction in sepsis []. NETs can serve as a scaffold for the entrapment and aggregation of platelets and red blood cells, thereby promoting coagulation and thrombosis. This function is mediated by the binding of NETs to proteins such as fibrinogen, fibronectin, and von Willebrand factor. Therefore, the disassembly of NETs can reduce thrombosis in animal models [].
Pediatric considerations: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) play an especially prominent role in pediatric sepsis. Children with sepsis have significantly higher serum concentrations of NETs than adults, and NET levels positively correlate with disease severity. The exaggerated NETosis in children may contribute to the simultaneous multi‑organ dysfunction and early mortality observed in this population. Additionally, neonatal neutrophils exhibit lower TLR4 expression and impaired chemotaxis due to reduced downstream signaling molecules (e.g., MyD88), which limits early cytokine responses but does not prevent late NET‑mediated tissue damage.

### Induce apoptosis of lymphocytes
Studies have shown that neutrophils have a negative regulatory effect on lymphocytes []. Sepsis induces the upregulation of programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) in neutrophils. PD-L1 + neutrophils have lower levels of cluster of differentiation 11a (CD11a), cluster of differentiation 62 ligand (CD62L), and C-C chemokine receptor type 2 (CCR2), while having higher levels of cluster of differentiation 16 (CD16) and cluster of differentiation 64 (CD64). This phenotypic change is associated with impaired migratory ability of neutrophils. Moreover, neutrophils can induce the apoptosis of lymphocytes through PD-L1 mediation.In clinical studies, it has also been found that the level of PD-L1 in neutrophils is negatively correlated with the level of human leukocyte antigen-DR (HLA-DR) in monocytes, and positively correlated with the severity of illness in septic patients. This implies that the upregulation of PD-L1 is involved in the process of sepsis-induced immunosuppression, and has an important impact on the development and prognosis of the disease [].

### Introduction
Pulmonary infections are a common cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, and can lead to serious complications such as sepsis or acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). International studies report that up to 70% intensive care unit (ICU) sepsis cases are due to pulmonary infections, including community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), COVID-19, and pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP). CAP cases continue to have significant mortality rates after hospitalisation, ranging from under 10% in patients under 60 to over 20% in those older than 60.
While pulmonary conditions such as CAP, COVID-19, PCP, ARDS, and septic shock of pulmonary origin have distinct pathophysiology, they all share a critical feature in that the mortality and morbidity rates are driven by dysregulated inflammatory pathways, diffuse alveolar damage, and systemic consequences such as shock. Pathogen recognition activates both proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory mediators, and an imbalance in these mediators leads to overproduction of proinflammatory cytokines and subsequent organ damage. Therefore, while triggers may differ, the downstream pathophysiology relevant to corticosteroid action converges.
During an infectious episode, glucocorticoids are released into the systemic circulation to restore immune homeostasis, achieved by inhibiting transcriptional regulators of proinflammatory effectors. At high doses, glucocorticoids act via non-genomic mechanisms, leading to reduced cytokine production. Early randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluated the efficacy of high-dose corticosteroids in septic shock, but failed to demonstrate a benefit between treatment and placebo groups.
Recent studies have transitioned to low-dose corticosteroid regimens. Evidence shows this approach provides medical advantages for certain respiratory conditions, including septic shock, severe CAP, and COVID-19. Guidelines currently endorse corticosteroid treatment (150 mg hydrocortisone-equivalent daily) for severe COVID-19 and conditionally approve it for septic shock and ARDS.
The current recommendations for severe CAP treatment show variable approaches. The American Thoracic Society (ATS) and British Thoracic Society do not support corticosteroid therapy in severe CAP, but European and Latin American guidelines suggest corticosteroids (methylprednisolone, 0.5 mg/kg every 12 hours for 5 days) for patients with severe CAP showing signs of shock. South African guidelines recommend corticosteroids as an adjunct to antibiotics in CAP admitted to the ICU.

### Objectives
To evaluate the effectiveness of low-dose corticosteroids in reducing short-term (90-day) mortality, by treating critically ill adults with severe pulmonary infections such as COVID-19, CAP, PCP, sepsis of pulmonary origin, septic shock, and ARDS. Thus, we include the most recent RCTs to assist in informing future clinical guidelines on steroid therapy.

### Methods
This meta-analysis was conducted according to a pre-registered protocol on the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO, ID: CRD42024627881).

### Search strategy
We used OVID to search two databases (Embase and Medline) from January 1990 to December 2024, with no restriction on publication status, but including English-language articles only. Search terms used included “steroid”, “sepsis”, “pneumonia”, “covid”, “critical care” (full search can be found in the electronic  detail, ESM). We included only RCTs, with a population of adults with severe pulmonary infections (COVID-19, CAP, sepsis, septic shock, ARDS, and PCP). Adults must be ≥18 years, and the severity of the pulmonary infections must be defined as ‘severe’ in each study, with specified parameters (). Patients must be treated with low-dose corticosteroids (≤400 mg hydrocortisone-equivalent daily) and have a comparable group treated with placebo or standard care. Although no single agreed-upon definition of low-dose corticosteroids exists for severe pulmonary infections, this cut-off follows recently published systematic reviews and meta-analyses looking at mortality effects in severe pulmonary infection. This upper threshold enables us to capture the majority of studies employing a low-dose regimen. Our primary outcome was short-term mortality (≤90 days). Our secondary outcomes were 28-day mortality, 30-day mortality, number of patients with at least one serious adverse event (SAE), length of hospital stay and ICU stay. Studies must also report at least one of the primary or secondary outcomes listed. Studies in which the patient population was not limited to pulmonary sources of infection, but in which outcome data could be identified as a subgroup analysis, were also included. Studies were excluded if there was a mixed population of severity. SAEs were defined individually by each included study. We also performed a manual search of reference lists of previous review articles, with the search completed on 8 December 2024. Two blinded investigators (JL, SH) screened articles for inclusion based on study title and abstract, and then relevant articles were retrieved for full text screening. All screened articles were able to be retrieved. This was reviewed again by two blinded investigators (HS, SG), and any conflicts were resolved by a third reviewer (JL).

### Data extraction
Two investigators (SH, MT) extracted all variables using a standardised template, including study characteristics, population demographics, interventions, and outcome data.

### Data synthesis and statistical analysis
Data were pooled by one investigator (JL), using the random-effects model; dichotomous outcomes (short-term mortality) were summarised as ORs, and continuous outcomes (length of hospital/ICU stay) were expressed as mean differences. For dichotomous data, the inverse variance method was used, and for continuous data, the combination method, Hedges’ g, was used.

The restricted maximum-likelihood estimator was used to derive between‐study variance (τ²). Meta-regression analyses were used to assess the effects of duration (as factor variables), and dose of steroids (as continuous variables). We also analysed duration by comparing short treatment duration (≤7 days) to long treatment duration (>7 days). For the dose of corticosteroid treatment, we compared >200 mg/day hydrocortisone-equivalent to ≤200 mg/day.

### Appraisal of the evidence
We assessed the certainty of the evidence using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) domains: risk of bias, heterogeneity, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias. This was done by JL and SH for each outcome.
Two investigators (JL, HS) evaluated bias for each study using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool, with any discrepancies settled by a third investigator (SH). This tool assesses bias in five domains, and provides an overall grade. Risk of bias was only assessed as low for each study if all domains were deemed as low risk. A single domain listed as high risk meant that the overall risk of bias was deemed as high risk.
Heterogeneity was assessed using χ² (Cochrane’s Q) test and quantified by the I² statistic, with additional parameters (τ and H). We then categorised heterogeneity into four groups according to the Cochrane Collaboration definitions: 0–40% might not be important; 30–60% may represent moderate heterogeneity; 50–90% may represent substantial heterogeneity; and 75–100% considerable heterogeneity.
Publication bias was assessed using Egger’s test and inspection of a funnel plot.

### Sensitivity and subgroup analyses
Sensitivity analyses included leave‐one‐out diagnostics, influence analyses, and a separate analysis including only RCTs at low risk of bias.
We assessed subgroups for short-term mortality according to aetiology of respiratory infection: COVID-19, CAP and sepsis, ARDS, and septic shock.

### INTRODUCTION
Sepsis and septic shock are life-threatening conditions caused by invasive micro-organisms and consequent immune and inflammatory responses (). One of the critical early investigations indicated for emergency department (ED) patients with sepsis is blood culture (BC), the gold-standard test for identifying causative micro-organisms in the bloodstream. This enables targeted antimicrobial therapy, ensuring pathogens are eradicated, abating deleterious inflammatory responses, and decreasing associated mortality (, ).
Current methods of BC collection, processing, and analysis have changed little in the last 50 years. Actionable results are not available to guide initial ED workup, and final results may not be available for several days (). Moreover, BC-based methods are known to have limited sensitivity, particularly in cases of recent exposure to antimicrobials, potentially leading to “culture-negative” sepsis episodes (, ). As a result, many patients remain on broad-spectrum antibiotics for extended courses. This is associated with the development of multidrug-resistant bacteria, drug side effects, and complications such as antibiotic-associated colitis ().
Developing alternative means for identifying pathogenic bacteria in the bloodstream is an active field of research with some promising developments (). However, most emerging methods rely on BCs to initially amplify bacterial numbers in the blood before analysis, a step that usually takes 8-12 hours ().
The T2 magnetic resonance system (T2 Biosystems, Lexington, MA, USA) uses PCR amplification and magnetic resonance-based molecular diagnostic technology to identify selected pathogenic microbial elements directly from whole blood, with results reportedly available in 3–9 h (). The T2Bacteria (T2B) panel detects six pathogenic bacteria—, and —which collectively account for 50%–60% of pathogens reported from BCs taken from patients in Australian EDs (, ). Some studies have shown T2 magnetic resonance more sensitive than BC, particularly in patients exposed to antimicrobials (, ).
Although early studies examining the clinical performance of T2B provided encouraging results (), further data are required to establish accuracy and clinical utility. Several studies have been limited by cohorts with low prevalence of positive BCs and low-quality comparator BC techniques (). To date, no data have been gathered in the Australian ED setting. The aim of this study was to assess the performance of the novel T2B panel for detection of bacteremia in ED patients at high risk for bloodstream infection.

### MATERIALS AND METHODS

### Setting
This prospective observational study was conducted in the ED of an Australian urban tertiary referral hospital treating 85,000–90,000 adult presentations annually. Patient enrollment occurred between February 2023 and February 2024. Approval was granted by the local ethics committee (HREC/2023/MNHA/94258) and ratified by the University of Queensland (2025/). All recruited subjects or their representatives consented to participation.

### Aims
Specific study questions were as follows:

### Subjects
Adult patients aged >18 years old presenting to the ED with suspected bloodstream infection and hypoperfusion (systolic blood pressure [SBP] <90 mmHg or lactate ≥4.0 mmol/L) were eligible for enrollment. Investigation and treatment of these patients proceeded as per departmental guidelines based on current evidence (), including two sets of BCs, other cultures as appropriate, organ support interventions, and antimicrobial therapy. Based on prior work, 35% of patients enrolled in the study were expected to have positive BCs, and in total 55% were expected to have any positive microbiological test (). The study sample size of 100 patients was determined by available funding for T2B analysis.

### Measurements
BCs were collected in BacT/Alert FA PLUS and FN PLUS bottles and incubated with the BacT/Alert Virtuo (bioMérieux, France) system for up to 5 days. Samples from positive culture bottles were Gram stained, plated, and further incubated for a maximum of 48 h. BCs were plated on blood, chocolate, and MacConkey agar. In the case of growth from the anaerobic bottle, anaerobic media were additionally inoculated. Additionally, one drop from positive BCs was applied to a chocolate agar plate and incubated for 4–6 h (CHOC spot). Pathogens growing on plates (including from the CHOC spot) underwent species identification with matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) (VITEK MS, bioMerieux, France) and susceptibility testing with VITEK 2 (bioMerieux, France). For each positive BC, data collected included time to Gram stain result and time to pathogen identification with MALDI-TOF MS.
Samples for T2B analysis were drawn in EDTA tubes and frozen at −70°C according to the freezing procedure allowed by the T2B package insert (). After recruitment of 101 study patients, samples were thawed and retrospectively batch analyzed, otherwise as per manufacturer specifications. Specifically, 2 mL of whole blood from each sample was pipetted into the T2B cartridge. Time to result was recorded for each T2B sample.
For each patient, clinical and microbiological data were abstracted from hospital records, databases of hematology, biochemistry, and microbiological results, and imaging as relevant. Times of antimicrobial administration, BC collection, and T2B sample collection were recorded. BC contamination was defined according to standard definitions ().

### Analyses
Analyses were performed using Stata, version 17 (StataCorp LLC). Baseline continuous variables were presented as mean (SD) or median (IQR), and categorical variables as  (%). Categorical variables were compared using Fisher’s exact test or Chi-squared test as appropriate. Continuous variables were compared using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Diagnostic accuracy statistics (sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value [PPV], and negative predictive value [NPV]) were calculated with 95% confidence intervals.
The potential role of T2B in supporting early adjustment of antimicrobials was assessed. To this respect, de-escalation was broadly defined as any potential change of empirical antimicrobials to remove unnecessary coverage based on T2B results (i.e., removal of Gram-positive coverage in the case of identification of Gram-negative pathogens and vice versa). Similarly, escalation was defined as any potential change of antimicrobials to add coverage of pathogens identified by the T2B against which empirical therapy was not effective (e.g., introduction of vancomycin in the case of detection of  or introduction of anti-pseudomonal therapy in the case of detection of  if these pathogens were not covered by empirical regimens, respectively). Escalation and de-escalation were not defined based on suppositions on the susceptibility profile of the specific species identified (e.g., switch from piperacillin-tazobactam to ampicillin in the case of detection of ).

### RESULTS

### Patients’ characteristics and T2B diagnostic accuracy
There were 101 patients enrolled in the study; clinical characteristics are detailed in . Males comprised 56%, and median age was 69 years (IQR 57–78 years). The most common sources of infection were respiratory (32.7%) and urinary tract (23.8%). Eighty-nine patients (88.1%) had two sets of BCs collected, while 12 patients (11.9%) had one set of BCs collected. After excluding contaminants, BCs were positive in 35 (34.7%) patients. Of these, five had polymicrobial growth, accounting for a total of 40 isolates grown according to conventional BC methods. The T2B assay identified 28 pathogens from 23 (22.8%) patients, returned an invalid result in one case (failure of internal control), and failed to provide a result due to machine dysfunction in a further three cases.  shows the isolates grown from BCs with  ( = 12),  ( = 7),  ( = 6), and  ( = 5) being the most commonly identified isolates. One BC was positive for . Overall, isolates included on the T2B panel comprised 31/40 (77.5%) of all isolates grown on BC.
and  show BC and T2B results. Nineteen patients had pathogens identified by both BC and T2B (BC+/T2B+), and 15 had identical pathogens on both panels. The remaining four patients had a concordant pathogen detected by BC and T2B plus an additional pathogen detected by either of the two tests (two by BC and two by T2B). Fourteen patients grew bacteria on BC but were T2B negative (BC+/T2B−, 14%). Eight of these patients grew T2B on-panel bacteria in BC (8%). BCs were negative in four patients where the T2B identified organisms (BC−/T2B+, 4%). At the patient level, agreement between T2B and BC when considering all pathogens was 81.4%, with sensitivity 57.6% and specificity 93.8%. If considering only T2B on-panel pathogens, agreement was 87.6%, sensitivity was 70.4%, and specificity was 94.3%.  reports diagnostic accuracy measures for the T2B.

### MATERIALS AND METHODS
This systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with the Cochrane Collaboration Handbook for Systematic Review of Interventions and reported following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) Statement guidelines (, ); as it used previously published data without involving human participants, institutional review board approval and informed consent were not required, and the study adhered to the ethical standards of the World Medical Association Declaration of Helsinki (1975, as revised).

### Eligibility Criteria
We included RCTs directly comparing HFNC with NIV in adults (≥18 y) admitted to the ICU who were at high risk of reintubation. Eligible studies were required to report at least one predefined clinical outcome. High risk of reintubation was defined by the presence of one or more of the following: age older than 65 years, APACHE II score greater than 12 on the day of extubation, obesity (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m or race-specific BMI cutoff where applicable), poor secretion management, difficult or prolonged weaning, two or more comorbidities, acute heart failure requiring mechanical ventilation, COPD, airway patency problems, prolonged mechanical ventilation, or hypercapnia at the end of a spontaneous breathing trial.
We excluded observational studies, single-arm studies, conference abstracts, pediatric-only populations, trials comparing NIV with conventional oxygen therapy without a separate HFNC subgroup, and studies using HFNC adjunctively with NIV. The predefined primary outcome was short-term reintubation within 72 hours of extubation. Secondary outcomes included sepsis, nosocomial pneumonia, ICU length of stay, and ICU mortality. Although duration of mechanical ventilation was prespecified, formal analysis was not feasible due to limited data (reported in only two RCTs).
Prespecified subgroup analyses of reintubation were conducted, where data allowed, to enhance clinical relevance. Subgroups included very high-risk patients (≥4 risk factors), obese patients (operative vs. nonoperative), and patients with acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD) and hypercapnic respiratory failure. An additional subgroup restricted to high-quality studies (excluding trials at high RoB) was performed. Subgroup data were extracted from published or  (). Random-effects models were applied, estimating odds ratios for dichotomous and mean differences (MDs) for continuous outcomes. Formal statistical tests for interaction between subgroups were not performed; therefore, subgroup findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating. Secondary outcomes were analyzed when sufficient data were available.

### Search Strategies and Data Extraction
A comprehensive search of major databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane Central) was performed from inception to February 2026. The full search strategies for each database are provided in  (). Reference lists of relevant systematic reviews and included studies were also manually screened for additional eligible trials. Study selection was conducted in two stages: titles and abstracts were independently screened by two reviewers (N.N. and N.A.d.B.e.L.) to identify potentially eligible studies, followed by independent full-text review. Data extraction was performed independently and in duplicate by N.B.T. and Y.Z. using a standardized form, with forest plot data independently verified by H.D.T.L. and V.N.D.N. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion or, if needed, by a third reviewer (N.N.). This meta-analysis was prospectively registered on PROSPERO under ID: CRD420261289624 (registered January 20, 2026). Study selection and screening results are summarized in a PRISMA flow diagram ().
[Figure: Figure 1. — The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses flowchart () of study selection. HFNC = high-flow nasal cannula, NIV = noninvasive ventilation, RCT = randomized controlled trial.]

### Statistical Analysis
Two reviewers (N.B.T. and Y.Z.) independently extracted baseline characteristics (, ) and outcome data. Dichotomous outcomes were pooled as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% CIs. Continuous outcomes were analyzed as MDs, since all studies reported results in consistent units (days), which improves clinical interpretability compared with standardized mean differences. A difference of greater than or equal to 1 day was considered the minimal clinically important difference.
Heterogeneity was assessed using the  statistic and Cochrane  test, with  greater than 50% and  value of less than 0.10 indicating substantial heterogeneity. All meta-analyses used a random-effects model (DerSimonian and Laird) to account for within- and between-study variability. Statistical analyses were conducted in Review Manager (RevMan) version 5.4 (Cochrane Collaboration, Copenhagen, Denmark). Sensitivity analyses employed a leave-one-out approach, and subgroup analyses were performed when data allowed. Assessment of small-study effects was planned when greater than or equal to 10 studies were available for an outcome, using funnel plots and Egger’s regression test.

### Quality Assessment
Two independent reviewers (N.A.d.B.e.L and N.B.T.) assessed the RoB using the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool (Bristol Medical School, Bristol, United Kingdom) (), across five domains: randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of outcomes, and selection of reported results. Each domain was rated as low, high, or unclear risk, with discrepancies resolved by consensus or a third reviewer (N.N.). Publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and, if uncertain, further assessed with Egger’s test (D.D.).
The certainty of evidence was appraised using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) () approach by (V.H.Q.T. and Y.Z.), considering risk of bias, imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness, and publication bias. Outcomes were rated as high, moderate, low, or very low certainty. All outcomes were evaluated to determine the overall strength and reliability of the HIGH-FLOW OXY meta-analysis findings.

### RESULTS

### Study Selection and Baseline Characteristics
The literature search identified 868 records. After removing duplicates and screening titles and abstracts, 30 studies underwent full-text review. Ten studies were excluded: two conference abstracts (, ), three ongoing trials (–), three studies that alternated NIV with HFNC (–), one post hoc analysis lacking standalone HFNC subgroup data (), and two trials without relevant outcomes (, ) (, ). Ultimately, 15 RCTs (, , –), including one post hoc analysis of Hernández et al (), met inclusion criteria, enrolling 2073 critically ill patients with predefined extubation failure risk factors (Fig. ).
Across the included trials, HFNC and NIV were evaluated as postextubation respiratory support strategies in critically ill patients at high risk of extubation failure.
All trials enrolled high-risk patients, with prespecified subpopulations including AECOPD with hypercapnic respiratory failure (, , , , ), very high-risk patients (≥4 risk factors) (, ), elderly (>65 y) (), obese patients (, , ), patient at high risk (<4 risk factors) (, ), patients with APACHE II greater than or equal to 12 (, ), and those with greater than or equal to 2 comorbidities (). Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were broadly similar across treatment groups, with more than 50% of participants being male. Median APACHE II scores were greater than or equal to 10 in 10 trials, indicating moderate-to-high illness severity (Supplementary Table 1, ). entries.clinicalQuestion_ko: 신속연속기관삽관(RSI)이 필요한 중증 성인 환자에서 ketamine이 propofol보다 유도 후 혈역학적 안정성, 특히 유도 후 첫 10분 내 최저 mean arterial pressure(MAP) 측면에서 더 나은 유도 진정제인가?

pico.population: [Country NR] Adults (≥ 18 years) requiring RSI in two mixed ICUs; 207 patients randomized and 175 included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (Ketamine 91, propofol 84), enrolled from October 2021 to October 2023. Exclusion: pregnancy, intubation during cardiac arrest, known/suspected intracranial hypertension, allergy to study drugs (lidocaine, fentanyl, propofol, ketamine, rocuronium), bradycardia (HR < 50) or AV block without pacemaker.
pico.intervention: Ketamine as the induction hypnotic agent for RSI, assigned 1:1 (open-label).
pico.comparison: Propofol as the induction hypnotic agent for RSI, assigned 1:1 (open-label).
pico.outcome: Primary outcome: lowest MAP within the first 10 min after induction, analyzed with a linear regression model adjusted for age, baseline MAP, and total vasopressor dose within 10 min. pico.population: [International] Patients within the first 4 hours of septic shock (Sepsis-3: suspected/confirmed infection plus hyperlactatemia and norepinephrine requirement due to persistent hypotension after ≥1000 mL fluid load in 1 hour) enrolled at 86 centers in 19 countries between March 2022 and April 2025 (last follow-up July 2025); from 1501 randomized, 1467 were included in the primary analysis (mean age, 66 [17] years; 43.3% female).
pico.intervention: CRT-PHR (n = 720), a personalized hemodynamic resuscitation protocol including assessment of pulse pressure, diastolic arterial pressure, fluid responsiveness, and bedside echocardiography, to tailor fluids, vasopressors, and inotropes.
pico.comparison: Usual care (n = 747).
pico.outcome: Hierarchical composite of mortality, duration of vital support (vasoactives, mechanical ventilation, and kidney replacement therapy), and length of hospital stay assessed at 28 days, analyzed by win ratio stratified by median APACHE II score: 131 131 wins (48.9%) in CRT-PHR vs 112 787 (42.1%) in usual care, win ratio 1.16 (95% CI, 1.02-1.33; P = .04). Individual wins — death 19.1% vs 17.8%; duration of vital support 26.4% vs 21.1%; length of hospital stay 3.4% vs 3.2%.

pico_ko.intervention: CRT-PHR(n = 720): pulse pressure, diastolic arterial pressure, fluid responsiveness, bedside echocardiography 평가를 포함해 수액·혈압상승제·강심제를 맞춤 조절하는 개인 맞춤형 혈역학 소생술 프로토콜.
pico_ko.comparison: Usual care(n = 747).
pico_ko.outcome: 28일 시점의 사망률, 생명유지치료 기간(vasoactives, mechanical ventilation, kidney replacement therapy), 재원기간의 계층적 복합 결과를 median APACHE II 점수로 층화한 win ratio로 분석: CRT-PHR 131 131 wins(48.9%) vs usual care 112 787(42.1%), win ratio 1.16(95% CI, 1.02-1.33; P = .04). 개별 wins — 사망 19.1% vs 17.8%; 생명유지치료 기간 26.4% vs 21.1%; 재원기간 3.4% vs 3.2%.

keyFindings: The hierarchical composite primary outcome favored CRT-PHR with 131 131 wins (48.9%) vs 112 787 (42.1%) in usual care, win ratio 1.16 (95% CI, 1.02-1.33; P = .04).
The benefit was driven primarily by a lower duration of vital support (individual wins 26.4% vs 21.1%), not by mortality (death wins 19.1% vs 17.8%) or length of hospital stay (3.4% vs 3.2%).
The trial was large and pragmatic — 86 centers in 19 countries, 1501 randomized (720 CRT-PHR vs 747 usual care), 1467 in the primary analysis (mean age 66 [17] years, 43.3% female).
keyFindings_ko: 계층적 복합 일차 결과는 CRT-PHR에 유리하여 131 131 wins(48.9%) vs usual care 112 787(42.1%), win ratio 1.16(95% CI, 1.02-1.33; P = .04)였다.
이득은 주로 짧아진 생명유지치료 기간(개별 wins 26.4% vs 21.1%)에서 비롯되었고, 사망(19.1% vs 17.8%)이나 재원기간(3.4% vs 3.2%)에서는 아니었다.
이 시험은 대규모 실용적 연구로 19개국 86개 센터에서 1501명 무작위 배정(720명 CRT-PHR vs 747명 usual care), 일차 분석 1467명(평균 연령 66 [17]세, 43.3% 여성)이었다.
